definition: Something that has to be true for a step of the reasoning to hold: the logframe's assumptions column, and the condition on an arrow in a theory of change (TAXONOMY.md D12). It sits on the link between two levels of the work, so it is named where that link is: a programme's pathway step, or a project's success criterion that rests on deliverables. It is stated once and named by every step it conditions. An assumption is not a risk: a risk is something that might go wrong and is mitigated; an assumption is tested, and if it turns out false the answer is a different theory, not a contingency. It is not a constraint (a fixed limit on the work), not a dependency (something the work waits on), and not a hope about the work's own effort.

/metadata/name.guide: A short title for the assumption, as a reader would scan it in a list: the condition in a few words.
good: Depots release staff for training during the season
A fault found at intake can still be put right

poor.why: Names a topic, not the condition; a reader cannot tell what is assumed.

/spec/statement.guide: What has to be true, in one sentence, present tense, about the world rather than about the work, stated so somebody could find out whether it is.
good: Depots let checkers off the floor for a training day while produce is still coming in.
Produce failing a check at intake can be sorted, repacked or cooled on the same day rather than written off.
Retail buyers price a supplier on how consistent its deliveries are, not only on the best of them.

poor.text: We will arrange cover for checkers on training days.
poor.why: A plan for the work, not a condition in the world. Say what has to be true (depots release staff), not what the team will do.

poor.text: The scanners might break during the pilot.
poor.why: Something that might go wrong is a risk, mitigated on the project's register, not an assumption.
Assumes the result it is meant to explain, and nobody could test it before the fact. Name the condition the step rests on.

poor.text: Depots release staff and buyers pay more for consistent produce.
poor.why: Two assumptions in one sentence; each conditions a different step and may fail on its own.

/spec/ifFalse.guide: What happens to the reasoning if this does not hold: which step stops working, and what that does to the change. An assumption nobody can say the consequence of is one nobody will act on.
good: Training waits for the closed season, so the shared standard arrives a season after the produce it was meant to grade.
Checking earlier finds the same faults sooner and loses the same produce, so the programme moves the paperwork and not the outcome.

poor.why: Too broad to act on; say which step stops working and what that does.
A mitigation, which belongs to a risk. This field says what the falsehood does to the reasoning.

/spec/confidence.guide: How sure anybody is that it holds: high, medium or low. A mark for a reader to weigh, never a number to multiply. Say in the note what the confidence rests on.

/spec/testedBy.guide: How anybody would find out, where there is a way: a KPI that would move, or a data source somebody could look in. An assumption is tested, where a risk is mitigated. Leave it empty when nothing Cartograph holds would show it, and say so in the note.

poor.why: Not a source anyone could look in again. Name the indicator or the data source that would show it.

/spec/note.guide: Anything else worth knowing, including where the assumption came from, who doubted it and why. Name roles or bodies, never persons.
good: The two pilot depots agreed; the rest were not asked.
Held by the market access team from two buyer conversations, not from a price schedule.

poor.why: Names a person and says nothing about what was checked. Name the role or team, and what they found.

Programme:/spec/pathway/-/assumes.ask: Which step of a programme's pathway does this have to hold for: which outcome would not follow from its preconditions if this were false?
Programme:/spec/pathway/-/assumes.ifNone: Write the pathway step first, on the programme: the outcome it reaches, the outcomes it rests on and why they produce it. Then name this assumption on that step.

Project:/spec/successCriteria/-/assumes.ask: Which project success criterion rests on this: which state would the deliverables fail to produce if this were false?
Project:/spec/successCriteria/-/assumes.ifNone: Write the success criterion first, on the project, with the deliverables it comes from. Then name this assumption on that criterion.
